passage.title: The Weaver's Iron Needles
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
High in the mist-wrapped peaks of the north stood the town of Oakhaven. There lived a master weaver named Talia. Once every ten years, a trader climbed the steep pass with a single spool of sun-gold thread. Any cloak woven from that gleaming thread would fetch a royal sum in the valley markets below. Talia had saved her silver coins for nine winters. She hoped to buy the golden spool and weave a banner fit for a king.

Two days before the trader arrived, an early gale howled down from the ice peaks. Freezing sleet tore through the sheep pens. It ripped the thick wool cloaks of the shepherds who guarded the flock. Worse still, a falling pine branch smashed the blacksmith's stone forge, snapping the town's last sewing needles in the rubble. Without strong needles to mend their torn wool cloaks, the shepherds could not face the coming snowstorm.

When the trader rode into the square at dawn, he held up the bright spool of golden thread in one hand. On his pack mule, though, rattled a leather pouch of forty tempered iron needles from the valley shops. Talia looked from the shining gold to the cold shepherds standing by the broken forge. The prized spool of golden thread, coveted for years by every merchant in the valley, was gladly passed over by Talia in exchange for the pouch of iron needles.

Before noon, Talia handed a sturdy iron needle to every home in Oakhaven. Neighbors met around her hearth with thick yarn spun from their own mountain sheep. Under Talia's steady hand, forty needles flashed in the firelight. Torn seams were pulled tight and patched with double layers of warm gray wool. While golden thread would have hung uselessly on a castle wall, rough wool and strong iron kept the wind from every door.

When the spring thaw finally opened the high pass, the shepherds brought Talia the finest, softest fleece from the new lambs. With her own iron needle, she wove a warm village cloth that hung in the hall for years. Talia never missed the palace gold she had left behind. She knew that the richest treasure in any mountain town was the craft that kept its people whole.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The prized spool of golden thread, coveted for years by every merchant in the valley, was gladly passed over by Talia in exchange for the pouch of iron needles."

Based on the structure of the sentence, who wanted the golden thread for years, and who chose to pass it up?

options.text: Talia coveted the iron needles for years, and every merchant in the valley passed over the golden thread.
Every merchant in the valley wanted the golden thread, and Talia passed it over for the iron needles.
The pouch of iron needles wanted the prized spool of golden thread for the palace.
The village blacksmith traded forty sheep to the merchant for a new stone forge.

questions.provingSentenceText: The prized spool of golden thread, coveted for years by every merchant in the valley, was gladly passed over by Talia in exchange for the pouch of iron needles.
questions.childTip: Follow both 'by' phrases: every merchant coveted the spool, while Talia passed it over.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'by every merchant in the valley' tells who desired ('coveted') the spool, while 'was gladly passed over by Talia' identifies the actor who turned it down.

What does the word coveted mean as it is used in Paragraph 3?

options.text: Greatly desired and wished for as a valuable prize
Thrown away into the mud because it was worthless

questions.provingSentenceText: The prized spool of golden thread, coveted for years by every merchant in the valley, was gladly passed over by Talia in exchange for the pouch of iron needles.
questions.childTip: Connect 'coveted' to the word 'prized' right before it and the royal fortune mentioned in Paragraph 1.
questions.parentExplanation: The adjective 'prized' and Paragraph 1's detail that the golden thread could 'fetch a royal fortune' show that 'coveted' means strongly desired or wished for.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, why are the villagers of Oakhaven unable to make new sewing needles themselves before the blizzard hits?

options.text: The village blacksmith had moved down to the valley markets the winter before.
A falling pine branch smashed the blacksmith's stone forge and snapped the town's last needles.
The shepherds traded all of the town's iron ore for royal banners.
No one in Oakhaven knew how to spin wool yarn from mountain sheep.

questions.provingSentenceText: Worse still, a falling pine branch smashed the blacksmith's stone forge, snapping the town's last sewing needles in the rubble.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 2 that explains what happened to the blacksmith's stone forge.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that a falling pine branch smashed the blacksmith's stone forge and snapped the town's last sewing needles in the rubble.

questions.prompt: How does Paragraph 4 contribute to the overall meaning of the folktale?

options.text: It contrasts the uselessness of a palace banner in a storm with the life-saving warmth of mended wool cloaks.
It explains how the merchant first found the spool of golden thread in a distant kingdom.
It shows that Talia regretted her trade and tried to buy back her silver coins.
It describes how the pine trees grew above the glaciers around Oakhaven.

questions.provingSentenceText: While golden thread would have hung uselessly on a castle wall, rough wool and strong iron kept the wind from every door.
questions.childTip: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 4 comparing golden thread on a castle wall to rough wool and strong iron.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 demonstrates the wisdom of Talia's sacrifice by contrasting decorative castle gold with practical iron needles and wool that protected every family from the winter wind.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which inference about Talia's character is best supported by the passage?

options.text: She cares far more about protecting her neighbors' lives than winning personal wealth or fame.
She dislikes weaving with wool and hopes to become a lowland blacksmith instead.
She only helps the shepherds because they promise to pay her double in gold coins.
She is afraid to let anyone else in Oakhaven touch her new iron needles.

questions.provingSentenceText: She knew that the richest treasure in any mountain town was the craft that kept its people whole.
questions.childTip: Think about why Talia gave up nine years of savings for needles she shared with every household.
questions.parentExplanation: Talia gives up her nine-year dream of palace wealth to buy iron needles for her neighbors, proving she values community survival over personal fortune (ELAGSE5RL1).
